title_original: Festival In Focus: Doha Gears Up For Lift-Off Against Geopolitical Odds: “It’s Not Smaller, We Have More Films & Guests”
excerpt_original: Organizing a film festival is a challenge at the best of times, figuring out the logistics with the threat of war on the doorstep requires an extra layer of resilience. It is a quality Fatma Al Remaihi, CEO of the Doha Film Institute (DFI) and her team have had to muster in…

blocks.text: Organizing a film festival is a challenge at the best of times, figuring out the logistics with the threat of war on the doorstep requires an extra layer of resilience. It is a quality Fatma Al Remaihi, CEO of the Doha Film Institute (DFI) and her team have had to muster in spades as they prepared for the second edition of the rebooted Doha Film Festival , setting in place logistics for a trio of different scenarios. “We knew that no matter what, we will have a festival… we were exploring differing scenarios, that it could be just for locals, that it could be for everyone, or that it could just be an online competition. We’ve planned for every eventuality,” Al Remaihi tells Deadline on the eve of the festival which is due to open on Thursday. She is speaking nine months after Israel and the U.S. launched a major military campaign against Iran’s Islamic Republic government at the end of February, which retaliated with missile and drone strikes on all its Gulf neighbours. The DFI was forced to move its popular annual Qumra project and talent incubator online in March, with the team applying lessons learned during the Covid-19 pandemic. While guests, including Gael García Bernal, Diego Luna and Alice Diop, could not make it to Qatar , Al Remaihi says the event still fulfilled its mission. “The filmmakers and the projects didn’t miss this edition. It was fantastic to be able to be there for them. Even though a lot of our staff here were suffering with scary times, they’re still pulled through and made it happen for the filmmakers.” The situation has calmed down since April and Qatar has been heavily involved in negotiations to deescalate the conflict, with its diplomats regularly traveling to the Iranian capital Tehran as part of international efforts to broker a peace deal. Al Remaihi is confident that the festival, running from November 19 to 27, will unfold at full capacity, alongside other events set to take place in Doha in the period including the Fashion Trust Arabia Awards on November 28 and the Formula 1 Grand Prix from November 27 to 28. “We’re so happy that we are a few days away from the festival, and excited now to open and experience it with everybody, and it’s not smaller, we have more films and more guests,” she says. The festival expands on the DFI’s long-running family-focused festival of Ajyal which ran for more than a decade during the same period, with Media City Qatar and the territory’s Film Committee coming on board as new partners as part of their mission to build the country’s media and entertainment sector. “I don’t like to call it a second edition as I don’t see it as a new festival. It’s a continuation of what we do,” notes Al Remaihi, while acknowledging that the repositioning gave the festival fresh impetus last year. The first edition of the reboot set the tone for a festival focused on cinema and rather than big name stars. “The guests that we invite are from the program. That’s what is important for us. They have a role in the program and something to give in the festival. It’s never been about big names and stars for us,” says Al Remaihi. She points nonetheless to the presence of Japanese director Naomi Kawase as jury president for the main International Competition; James Gray , for a gala screening of Paper Tiger , and Oscar-winning documentarian Gianfranco Rosi ,who is also on the jury alongside rising actor Adam Bessa, Tunisian producer Dora Bouchoucha and Palestinian director Kamal Aljafari.

blocks.text: Indian filmmaker and actor Nandita Das ( Manto , Zwigato ) and regional star, the Syrian actor Taim Hassan ( Al Hayba , Mawlana ), will also be in attendance to receive the festival’s Creative Excellence Award. “We have big names. Maybe for the public eyes, it’s different. But for people who work in the industry and who value filmmaking and the craft itself, they know these names and they’re very excited to have them in Doha. In that sense, I’m very happy with the caliber of the guests who are coming to the festival,” she explains.

blocks.caption: The Station Screen Project, Georges Films

blocks.text: DFI-backed Yemen-set drama The Station by Sara Ishaq – set against the backdrop of woman-only petrol stations in the war-torn country – opens this edition. “We confirmed The Station for the opening months ago. It’s very rare to have an opening film confirmed from that early, but we saw in this film everything that embodies the festival and the spirit of the festival,” says Al Remaihi. “It’s a simple story that sheds light on a very complicated background, and we thought it was very brave to make a film like this. We don’t see a lot coming out of Yemen. Yes, it had its premiere in Cannes, but we wanted to give it center stage in the festival.” The Station is among 15 films playing in the International Competition at the heart of the festival, competing for close to $200,000 in combined prize money. It features a raft of titles which have garnered acclaim on the festival circuit over the past year including Cameroonian director Auguste Bernard Kouemo’s House of the Wind , which won Venice’s Lion of the Future for a Debut Film when it premiered there in its Orizzonti sidebar in September. Further contenders include Moroccan director Tala Hadid’s Bardi , which played at the New York Film Festival, and Thai filmmaker Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s 9 Temples to Heaven , which premiered in Cannes Directors’ Fortnight and is Thailand’s submission to the 99th Academy Awards. Other Oscar hopefuls in the lineup include the Philippines’ entry Filipiñana by Rafael Manuel and Chilean director Manuela Martelli’s The Meltdown . There are four films by Palestinian filmmakers including Rabab Khamis’ documentary Sama , about a ten-year-old girl who collects plastic and cardboard in Deir al-Balah in Gaza to sell as fuel and help sustain her family, which world premieres It is joined by Hosam Abu Dan’s Gaza-shot drama Thirteen in Gaza , about a 13-year-old living with her father in a Gaza displacement camp, which won the NETPAC Award in Toronto; Muayad Alayan’s Venice–selected Conversation with the Sea , about a Palestinian man caught in the crosshairs of Israeli bureaucracy, and Mohanad Yaqubi’s Revolutionaries Never Die , revolving around 113 reels of films preserved by Lebanese filmmaker Jocelyne Saab. The final contenders are Asmahan Bkerat’s Concrete Land, Hugo Salvaterra’s My Semba, Zou Jing Cannes Critics’ Week Fipresci-winner A Girl Unknown , Alessandra Sanguinetti’s The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer and Alexander Murphy’s Tin Castle . Eleven of the films have received the support of the DFI’s grantee programs, with Al Remaihi explaining it is at the heart of an interconnected process developed over the institute’s 16-year existence. “It just shows that we don’t do anything on a singular basis. Everything we do is connected. We have an ecosystem that we built a long time ago, and we’ve seen the benefits of having something like this,” she says. “A lot of the films in our competition are grantees because it speaks to the type of funding that we do, choices that we make, the people that we work with, and we love to celebrate all of this during the festival with all of that community. It’s a great moment for us also to have all of that come together.” Outside of the competition, there will be gala screening for Paper Tige r, Rami Kodeih’s DFI-backed Beirut-set heist thriller Furies, Maiken Baird’s Toronto-selected Edward Said: Between Worlds and Bruno Dumont’s Red Rocks .

blocks.caption: Fatma Al Remaihi on the red carpet at the 2025 Doha Film Festival Getty Images

blocks.text: There will also be Special Screenings for Abderrahmane Sissako’s Artou , Daniele Rugo’s Life Support , following international doctors working alongside local medical staff in Gaza in 2023; Ginevra Elkann drama The Roses of Marrakech and Ali El Arabi’s 52 Blue .

Another key strand is the Made In Qatar sidebar. This has traditionally showcased short films but makes history this year as it premieres f our locally produced features , spanning Jodari Meno by Jamal Al Khanji, A Very Ordinary Life by Mohamed Deniz, First to Fly by Rodrigo Vazquez Salessi and When the News Breaks You by Hamad Al Hajri.

“It’s a testament to all of the work that we’ve been doing over the years and how the industry has developed in Qatar. We’ve been doing this for a long time, but now its not just the Doha Film Institute. We the Film Committee, Media City Qatar, and Katara Studios, all the film production houses,” she says. “You feel that there is a huge movement and a huge shift in the industry here.” A new addition is the Cinema Alkhaleej sidebar showcasing cinema from across the Gulf region, with highlights including the world premiere of horror feature Soulala by Saudi director and actor Hisham Fqih as well as the Qatar premiere of Ahd Kamel’s My Driver and I , which originally premiered at Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea International Film Festival in 2024. “We wanted to bring the Khaleeji (Gulf) industry together and have them more involved in the festival, not just as guests but also as participating guests. A lot of these films were not available here, so they are still fresh for our audiences. I loved watching all these films as we programmed the section and I’m excited to share them with the audience here.”
